commentary:
Energy is the morning's story, and it's a de-escalation trade. Crude turned lower overnight — Brent -1.5% toward $98 and WTI -2.3% to the low $90s — as markets tracked diplomatic efforts around Hormuz, with Washington signalling openness to Iran talks at the UN General Assembly and Saudi Arabia restarting the East-West pipeline, reopening a key Red Sea export route shut for two weeks after drone strikes. The whole curve is softening: prompt Brent spreads are the weakest in two weeks, put volumes have outpaced calls for three sessions, and the products complex followed — heating oil -1.7%, gasoil -2.2%, TTF -4.1%.

That said, the structural tightness story hasn't gone away: diesel is at record highs on strained refining capacity, and warnings of $150 Brent if disruption persists into 2027 keep the tail risk alive, according to reports. The macro backdrop remains the "5% world" — last week's Fed hike, the first in three years, reasserted credibility against oil-driven, supply-side sticky inflation, and huge AI-related financing demand is stacking on top of heavy government borrowing (the UK's £18.3bn August deficit underlines the fiscal strain, weighing on OATs and gilts sentiment).

Softer crude is doing the rates market's work today: Treasuries caught a bid across the curve with the long bond +0.3%, on the logic that good oil news lets yields fall. Equity index futures held the AI rally — S&P flat, Nikkei +2.1% on yen dynamics and the tech bid — while copper's +1.3% pop stands out against a soft metals tape, riding China's data-center buildout ambitions; gold eased with the risk premium.
